chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab, who said:

I made a vow for one of my sons that if Allah healed him, I would perform Hajj on foot. So I walked until I reached the 'Aqabah (pass), then I complained (of weakness), so I rode. Then I found ease, so I walked. I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that. He said: 'I like that if you are financially capable, you slaughter a cow.' I said: 'With me is the cost of a cow, and if I wished to slaughter, I would, but I have a debt.' He said: 'I like that if you are financially capable, you slaughter a cow.' I said: 'Is it something obligatory that I do?' He said: 'No. Whoever dedicates something to Allah and reaches his utmost capacity, there is no obligation upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a vow to perform Hajj on foot if one becomes unable to walk?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling for one who vows to perform Hajj on foot but becomes unable to complete it due to hardship. He indicates that slaughtering a cow is a recommended (mustahabb) expiation for the financially able, but not obligatory (wajib), establishing that fulfilling the vow to the extent of one's capacity ('juhd') suffices without further penalty. This ruling underscores the Shia principle of ease in fulfilling vows, distinguishing between the obligation of the act and the recommended compensation for inability.
